claim: Antagonistic interactions are widespread in the microbial world and affect microbial evolutionary dynamics.
source: Antagonistic interactions are widespread in the microbial world and affect microbial evolutionary dynamics.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature and the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Natural microbial communities often display spatial structure, which affects biological interactions.
source: Natural microbial communities often display spatial structure, which affects biological interactions, but much of what we know about microbial antagonism comes from laboratory studies of well-mixed communities.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in microbial ecology and is presented as background context.

claim: Two killer strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae were manipulated to express different toxins under independent control.
source: To overcome this limitation, we manipulated two killer strains of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, expressing different toxins, to independently control the rate at which they released their toxins.
evidence: This describes the experimental system developed by the authors, which is detailed in the methods and results sections.

claim: Mathematical models were developed that predict the experimental dynamics of competition between toxin-producing strains in both well-mixed and spatially structured populations.
source: We developed mathematical models that predict the experimental dynamics of competition between toxin-producing strains in both well-mixed and spatially structured populations.
evidence: The manuscript presents mathematical models (Equations 1-12) and shows their predictions match experimental data.

claim: A stronger antagonist can invade a weaker one only if the initial invading population exceeds a critical frequency or size.
source: In both situations, we experimentally verified theory's prediction that a stronger antagonist can invade a weaker one only if the initial invading population exceeds a critical frequency or size.
evidence: This is experimentally verified in Figures 3, 4, and 5, showing that invasion success depends on initial inoculum size.

claim: Toxin-resistant cells and weaker killers arose in spatially structured competitions between toxin-producing strains.
source: Finally, we found that toxin-resistant cells and weaker killers arose in spatially structured competitions between toxin-producing strains, suggesting that adaptive evolution can affect the outcome of microbial antagonism in spatial settings.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6, which shows the emergence of mutants with altered toxin production or resistance.

claim: Microbes often live in dense aggregates such as biofilms, which offer protection from environmental forces, drugs, and predation.
source: They often live in dense aggregates, such as biofilms, which offer them protection from environmental forces, drugs, and predation (Nadell et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nadell et al., 2016.

claim: Cooperation prevents the separation between different genotypes that occurs in range expansions.
source: For example, cooperation, in which two strains feed each other amino acids, prevents the separation between different genotypes (Müller et al., 2014) that occurs when two non-interacting populations spread across a surface in a range expansion (Hallatschek et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Müller et al., 2014 and Hallatschek et al., 2007.

claim: Antagonistic interactions are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: Antagonistic interactions are found in both prokaryotes (Atanasova et al., 2013; Cheung et al., 1997; Riley and Wertz, 2002; Veening and Blokesch, 2017) and eukaryotes (Boynton, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The ability of two Vibrio cholerae strains to kill each other using the type VI secretion system coarsens single-strain domains of initially well-mixed populations.
source: On an agar plate, the ability of two Vibrio cholerae strains to kill each other, using the type VI secretion system, coarsens the single-strain domains of populations that were initially well mixed (McNally et al., 2017; Yanni et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McNally et al., 2017 and Yanni et al., 2019.

claim: Theoretical models predict that cooperators require each other to prosper.
source: Theoretical models predict different outcomes for cooperation and antagonism: cooperators require each other to prosper (Müller et al., 2014) and antagonistic interactions lead to the competitive exclusion of one of the antagonists (Lavrentovich and Nelson, 2019; Nowak et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Antagonistic interactions lead to the competitive exclusion of one of the antagonists.
source: Theoretical models predict different outcomes for cooperation and antagonism: cooperators require each other to prosper (Müller et al., 2014) and antagonistic interactions lead to the competitive exclusion of one of the antagonists (Lavrentovich and Nelson, 2019; Nowak et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: The strain that survives in a 1:1, well-mixed culture is referred to as the stronger antagonist.
source: We refer to the strain that survives in a 1:1, well-mixed culture as the stronger antagonist and the one that goes extinct as the weaker antagonist.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for clarity in the manuscript.

claim: Models based on generalizations of the Lotka-Volterra equations predict that being a stronger antagonist is necessary but not sufficient for an invading strain to replace a resident antagonist population.
source: Models based on generalizations of the Lotka-Volterra equations (Lavrentovich and Nelson, 2019; Tanaka et al., 2017) predict that being a stronger antagonist is a necessary, but not a sufficient condition for an invading strain to replace a resident, antagonist population: successful replacement requires that the initial inoculum of the invading antagonist be larger than a critical frequency (i.e., relative abundance) in well-mixed populations or a critical size in spatially structured populations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models by Lavrentovich and Nelson, 2019 and Tanaka et al., 2017.

claim: Successful replacement of a resident antagonist population requires that the initial inoculum of the invading antagonist be larger than a critical frequency in well-mixed populations or a critical size in spatially structured populations.
source: Models based on generalizations of the Lotka-Volterra equations (Lavrentovich and Nelson, 2019; Tanaka et al., 2017) predict that being a stronger antagonist is a necessary, but not a sufficient condition for an invading strain to replace a resident, antagonist population: successful replacement requires that the initial inoculum of the invading antagonist be larger than a critical frequency (i.e., relative abundance) in well-mixed populations or a critical size in spatially structured populations.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that is experimentally tested in the manuscript.

claim: The requirement for a critical inoculum size implies that mutations conferring increased strength of antagonism may not establish in a population if the mutant population size is below a threshold.
source: The prediction of a critical size has implications for the population dynamics of antagonistic interactions: the requirement for a critical inoculum size implies that mutations conferring an increased strength of antagonism may not necessarily establish in a population because of a deterministic push to extinction if the population size of the mutant is below a given threshold.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the theoretical prediction of critical inoculum size.

claim: The critical size predicts that populations of weaker antagonists should be resistant to invasion from a stronger antagonist below a certain rate of immigration.
source: Conversely, the critical size predicts that populations of weaker antagonists should be resistant to invasion from a stronger antagonist, at least below a certain rate of immigration.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical model regarding invasion dynamics.

claim: Two strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae were engineered to express two different toxins from two different inducible promoters.
source: We developed an experimental system in which two strains of the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, expressed two different toxins from two different, inducible promoters (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1A, which illustrates the genetic constructs.

claim: The dynamics of competitive exclusion were investigated in three environments: spatially well-mixed populations in liquid cultures, spatially well-mixed populations on surfaces, and spatially structured populations on surfaces.
source: We investigated the dynamics of competitive exclusion in three environments: spatially well-mixed populations in liquid cultures or on surfaces, and spatially structured populations on surfaces.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Mathematical models of population dynamics regulated by toxin production and toxin-induced cell death were derived and parametrized using competition assays.
source: We derived mathematical models of population dynamics regulated by toxin production and toxin-induced cell death and parametrized them using competition assays between toxin-producing ('killer') cells and sensitive, nonkiller ones (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Experiments verified theoretical predictions on the conditions that lead to successful invasion of an antagonistic strain in all three environments.
source: Experiments verified theoretical predictions on the conditions that lead to a successful invasion of an antagonistic strain in all three environments (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The mathematical models correctly predict the dynamics of competition between toxin-producing strains in all scenarios considered.
source: The mathematical models correctly predict the dynamics of competition between toxin-producing strains in all scenarios considered here, they highlight the processes that lead to a region devoid of cells between two antagonistic strains that encounter each other on a solid surface, and can guide attempts to manipulate naturally occurring microbial communities.
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the results section with comparisons between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The models highlight the processes that lead to a region devoid of cells (halo) between two antagonistic strains on a solid surface.
source: The mathematical models correctly predict the dynamics of competition between toxin-producing strains in all scenarios considered here, they highlight the processes that lead to a region devoid of cells between two antagonistic strains that encounter each other on a solid surface, and can guide attempts to manipulate naturally occurring microbial communities.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 and discussed in the section on spatial models.

claim: Strain K1 expresses the killer toxin K1.
source: The two killer strains expressed two different killer proteins (Tipper and Bostian, 1984) that do not confer immunity to each other: strain K1 expresses the killer toxin K1 (Bevan and Makower, 1963) and strain K2 expresses the killer toxin K2 (Naumova and Naumova, 1973).
evidence: This describes the experimental strains used in the study.

claim: Strain K2 expresses the killer toxin K2.
source: The two killer strains expressed two different killer proteins (Tipper and Bostian, 1984) that do not confer immunity to each other: strain K1 expresses the killer toxin K1 (Bevan and Makower, 1963) and strain K2 expresses the killer toxin K2 (Naumova and Naumova, 1973).
evidence: This describes the experimental strains used in the study.

claim: Killer cells are immune to the toxin they produce because the unprocessed toxins confer immunity.
source: Killer cells are immune to the toxin they produce because the unprocessed toxins confer immunity (Dignard et al., 1991; Hanes et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dignard et al., 1991 and Hanes et al., 1986.

claim: Both the K1 and K2 killer toxins bind to β-1,6-glucans on the cell wall.
source: Both the K1 and K2 killer toxins bind to β-1,6-glucans on the cell wall, and subsequently translocate to the cytoplasmic membrane where they bind to a secondary receptor (Kre1p for K1, an unknown receptor for K2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of these toxins.

claim: Both K1 and K2 toxins disrupt the cytoplasmic membrane increasing its permeability to ions.
source: Both K1 and K2 disrupt the cytoplasmic membrane increasing its permeability to ions (Magliani et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magliani et al., 1997.

claim: Increasing the concentration of galactose increased the rate at which the frequency of K1 grew with time in competition assays.
source: Increasing the concentration of galactose increased the rate at which the frequency of K1 grew with time.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2, which displays experimental data on killer vs. sensitive competitions.

claim: For strain K2, increasing the concentration of copper increased the rate at which the strain's frequency grew with time.
source: Increasing the concentration of copper increased the rate at which the two strains' frequencies grew with time; the less fluorescent strain K2b was a weaker killer than the more fluorescent strain K2 at all copper concentrations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2, which displays experimental data.

claim: The less fluorescent strain K2b was a weaker killer than the more fluorescent strain K2 at all copper concentrations.
source: Increasing the concentration of copper increased the rate at which the two strains' frequencies grew with time; the less fluorescent strain K2b was a weaker killer than the more fluorescent strain K2 at all copper concentrations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 by comparing the killing rates of K2 and K2b.

claim: In the absence of inducers, the K1 strain frequency remained constant in competition assays.
source: In the absence of the inducer, galactose, the frequency of K1 remained constant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 for the 0 µM galactose condition.

claim: Strains K2 and K2b displayed killing activity even in the absence of copper, consistent with leaky expression from the PCUP1 promoter.
source: For both strains, their relative frequency increased with time even in the absence of copper, which is consistent with leaky expression from the PCUP1 promoter (Butt et al., 1984; Gorman et al., 1986) in the absence of added copper.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations to Butt et al., 1984 and Gorman et al., 1986.

claim: There is no correlation between the frequency at the first and second measurement time point for replicates initialized close to the unstable equilibrium.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows that there is no correlation between the frequency at the first and second measurement time point for those replicates that were initialized close to the unstable equilibrium (i.e., data points at 250 µM galactose in Figure 3D), suggesting that the stochasticity of the dynamics dominates over the initial condition when determining which replicates tend toward different stable equilibria in the long-term limit.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: All K1 populations whose initial area was below 12 mm² were outcompeted by the K2b lawn and driven to extinction.
source: As shown in Figure 5B–D, all K1 populations whose initial area was below 12 mm2 were outcompeted by the K2b lawn and driven to extinction, whereas all those whose initial area was above 12 mm2 managed to persist and eventually expanded displacing the resident K2b population (except for one outlier population highlighted in Figure 5B–D with a gray arrow and gray lines, which we discuss separately below).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B-D, which displays experimental data from spatially structured populations.

claim: All K1 populations whose initial area was above 12 mm² managed to persist and eventually expanded displacing the resident K2b population.
source: As shown in Figure 5B–D, all K1 populations whose initial area was below 12 mm2 were outcompeted by the K2b lawn and driven to extinction, whereas all those whose initial area was above 12 mm2 managed to persist and eventually expanded displacing the resident K2b population (except for one outlier population highlighted in Figure 5B–D with a gray arrow and gray lines, which we discuss separately below).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Most populations exhibited an initial retreat of both strains, leaving a region devoid of cells (halo) at the outer edge of the initial inoculum, followed by expansion of the K1 strain.
source: Most of the populations exhibited two characteristic phases in their spatial dynamics (Figure 5C–E): an initial retreat of both strains, leaving a region devoid of cells at the outer edge of the initial inoculum (black 'halos' in Figure 5E, of width 400±200 µm, mean ± SD), followed by the expansion of the K1 strain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-E, which displays experimental observations.

claim: The halo region had a width of 400±200 µm (mean ± SD).
source: Most of the populations exhibited two characteristic phases in their spatial dynamics (Figure 5C–E): an initial retreat of both strains, leaving a region devoid of cells at the outer edge of the initial inoculum (black 'halos' in Figure 5E, of width 400±200 µm, mean ± SD), followed by the expansion of the K1 strain.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: All inoculations below the critical inoculum size went extinct very rapidly.
source: All the inoculations below the critical inoculum size, instead, went extinct very rapidly (Figure 5A and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and F.

claim: A control experiment using nonkiller strains S1 and S2 showed that all inoculations maintained their area following successive transfers.
source: A control experiment performed in parallel using the two sensitive, nonkiller strains S1 and S2 shows that all inoculations maintained their area following successive transfers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The retreat and expansion dynamics and the dependence of invasion success on the size of the initial inoculum can be attributed to the antagonistic interactions engineered between strains K1 and K2b.
source: Thus, the retreat and expansion dynamics and the dependence of invasion success on the size of the initial inoculum can be attributed to the antagonistic interactions engineered between strains K1 and K2b.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the behavior of killer strains (Figure 5) with nonkiller controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: An outlier K1 population (K1o) decreased its area monotonically with time, unlike other populations.
source: An outlier K1 population (K1o) highlighted with a gray arrow and gray lines in Figure 5B–D (first row of Figure 6A) decreased its area monotonically with time, unlike all other populations that either went extinct or eventually expanded their area.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5B-D and 6A.

claim: The average fluorescent intensity of K1 cells sampled from the outlier replica K1o was reduced with respect to the ancestral K1 population.
source: Flow cytometry measurements of the fluorescent intensity of K1 cells sampled from the outlier replica K1o showed that their average fluorescent intensity was reduced with respect to the ancestral K1 population, and also compared to K1 cells sampled from a non-outlier population (K1s) that successfully expanded in the spatially structured experiments (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B, which displays flow cytometry data.

claim: The outlier population K1o was a weaker antagonist than K1 and K1s.
source: We tested the hypothesis that the outlier population K1o was a weaker antagonist by performing a competition assay in liquid medium, competing K1o against the ancestor K2b population and against the nonkiller strain S2, at 50:50 initial frequencies following the same protocol as the experiments of Figures 2 and 3A. In the same experiment, we competed the ancestor K1 and the successful invader, K1s, against the ancestor K2b (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, panel A) and against the nonkiller strain S2. We found that K1s and the ancestor K1 increased in frequency faster than K1o, demonstrating that the outlier population K1o was indeed a weaker antagonist than K1s and K1, which followed similar trajectories.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: K2b cells sampled from the region surrounding K1o (K2bo) followed the same dynamics as the original K2b stock in competition assays against K1.
source: Even though visual inspection of the spatiotemporal dynamics of K2b in the outlier replica suggest that this might have happened (cyan cells rapidly re-invaded the magenta K1o population from the top, see Figure 6A), competition assays between K1 and K2b cells sampled from the area surrounding K1o (K2bo) rule out this hypothesis, given that they followed the same dynamics of competition assays between the original K2b stock and K1 (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: K2b cells from a sub-population that re-invaded a K1 population (K2br) had greatly decreased sensitivity to the toxin produced by K1.
source: By competing K2b cells from the sub-population highlighted with the green arrow (K2bg) in Figure 5B against the ancestor K1 in competition assays in liquid media with 360 µM galactose, we found that they had greatly decreased (possibly null) sensitivity to the toxin produced by K1 (Figure 6D), suggesting that they became K1 resistant during the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No differences in growth rate were detected between any pairs of strains.
source: Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3 reveal that we could not detect any differences in growth rate between any pairs of strains, ruling out the possibility that the altered outcomes of competition observed in Figure 6 could be due to changes in cell division times during the experiment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The model that explicitly includes nutrient dynamics can reproduce the formation of the halo.
source: By exploring models with different levels of complexity and realism (Materials and methods), we found that we had to explicitly model the dynamics of nutrients (glucose) to reproduce the formation of the halo, which in the models consists of a region of mutual destruction, with significantly reduced cell density at the boundary between the two strains.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model parametrized using competition assays could reproduce the striking halos observed at the boundary between the two strains.
source: We found that this model, parametrized using the competition assays between toxin-producing and nonkiller strains and using suitable estimates for the diffusion coefficients of the nutrients, toxins, and yeast cells taken from the literature, could reproduce the striking halos observed at the boundary between the two strains (Figure 7A), suggesting that the halo emerges due to a combination of toxin-induced killing and diffusion of nutrients away from the agar beneath the halo and their consumption by the cells bordering the halo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The halo emerges due to a combination of toxin-induced killing and diffusion of nutrients away from the agar beneath the halo.
source: We found that this model, parametrized using the competition assays between toxin-producing and nonkiller strains and using suitable estimates for the diffusion coefficients of the nutrients, toxins, and yeast cells taken from the literature, could reproduce the striking halos observed at the boundary between the two strains (Figure 7A), suggesting that the halo emerges due to a combination of toxin-induced killing and diffusion of nutrients away from the agar beneath the halo and their consumption by the cells bordering the halo.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The model correctly predicts the extinction of smaller inoculations with a critical inoculum size between 8 and 14 mm².
source: Upon numerically integrating the model, starting from initial conditions comparable to those used in the experiments with spatially structured populations, we found that it correctly predicts the extinction of the smaller inoculations, with a critical inoculum size between 8 and 14 mm2, and the initial retreat and subsequent expansion of the larger ones (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The model predicts an enhanced density of the two killer strains at the two sides of the halo.
source: The model also predicts an enhanced density of the two killer strains at the two sides of the halo (Figure 7A), caused by the diffusion of glucose away from the agar underneath the halo to sustain cell growth at the exposed edges of the regions occupied by the two strains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and is an inference from the model.

claim: No further growth in the halo region was observed after transferring populations to 32°C, a temperature at which both toxins are unstable.
source: To test this, we experimentally verified that no further growth in the halo region is observed after transferring populations that competed for 48 hr at 25–32°C for further 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), a temperature at which both the K1 and K2 toxins are unstable and fail to inhibit the growth of susceptible strains (Marquina et al., 2002; Lukša et al., 2016, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The K1 and K2 toxins are unstable at 32°C and fail to inhibit the growth of susceptible strains.
source: To test this, we experimentally verified that no further growth in the halo region is observed after transferring populations that competed for 48 hr at 25–32°C for further 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), a temperature at which both the K1 and K2 toxins are unstable and fail to inhibit the growth of susceptible strains (Marquina et al., 2002; Lukša et al., 2016, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marquina et al., 2002 and Lukša et al., 2016, and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The appearance of mutations altered the outcome of competitions by changing the rate of toxin production or the sensitivity to toxin.
source: In our experiments, we saw the appearance of mutations that altered the outcome of competitions by either changing the rate of toxin production or the sensitivity to the toxin secreted by an antagonistic strain.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6, which shows mutants with altered phenotypes.

claim: The experimental system provides a synthetic model of microbial antagonism in which the interaction strength of two antagonist strains can be controlled independently and continuously.
source: Our work provides a synthetic model of microbial antagonism in which the interaction strength of two antagonist strains can be controlled independently and continuously, via titratable induction of promoters that respond to different chemicals.
evidence: This describes the key feature of the experimental system developed in this study.
